articles.subject: science
articles.title: What Is a Meadow?
articles.summary: A sunny grassy place full of plants, bugs, and birds.
articles.content:
A **meadow** is an open place where grasses and wildflowers grow. It is brighter and more open than a deep forest.

In a meadow you might see:
- Tall grass waving in the wind
- Colorful flowers
- Bees, butterflies, and birds

Meadows are important homes (**habitats**) for many small animals. When you explore a meadow in a game or outside, walk gently and look closely — tiny lives are busy all around you!

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Busy Bees and Pollination
articles.summary: How bees help plants make seeds and fruit.
articles.content:
Bees visit flowers to collect **nectar** (sweet liquid food) and **pollen**. As a bee moves from flower to flower, pollen sticks to its body and gets carried along.

That travel is called **pollination**. Many plants need pollination to make seeds and fruit. Without pollinators like bees, some crops and wild plants would struggle.

**Be kind to bees:**
- Don’t swat at them
- Leave wildflowers when you can
- Remember they are workers, not villains

Next time you see a bee on a blossom, you are watching a tiny delivery service for nature!

articles.subject: science
articles.title: How Plants Make Food
articles.summary: Photosynthesis in kid-friendly language.
articles.content:
Plants are amazing cooks that use light!

**Photosynthesis** is how green plants make food. They take in:
- **Sunlight**
- **Water** from the soil (through roots)
- **Carbon dioxide** from the air

Inside green leaves, plants build sugars they can use for energy and growth. As a bonus for animals and people, many plants release **oxygen** we breathe.

That is why forests, meadows, and gardens matter so much — they are living factories powered by the Sun.

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: The Water Cycle
articles.summary: How water moves from land to sky and back again.
articles.content:
Earth’s water is always on the move. This journey is called the **water cycle**.

1. **Evaporation** — The Sun heats water in rivers, lakes, and oceans. Some water turns into vapor and rises.
2. **Condensation** — Cooler air high up turns vapor into tiny droplets that form clouds.
3. **Precipitation** — Water falls as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
4. **Collection** — Water flows into streams, soaks into soil, or returns to larger bodies of water.

The same water has been cycling for a very long time. When it rains on a meadow, you are meeting an ancient traveler!

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: Rivers: Moving Water
articles.summary: What rivers are and why towns love them.
articles.content:
A **river** is fresh water that flows across the land. It usually starts in hills or mountains and travels toward a lake or the sea.

Rivers help people and animals by providing:
- Drinking water (after it is cleaned)
- Homes for fish
- Paths for boats
- Rich soil nearby for farming

In adventure games, a river can be a barrier — or a path if you find a bridge. In real life, rivers are precious, so we keep them clean.

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: Reading a Simple Map
articles.summary: Symbols, directions, and finding your way.
articles.content:
A **map** is a drawing of a place from above. Maps use **symbols** so they can show a lot of information in a small space.

Useful map parts:
- **Title** — what the map shows
- **Legend (key)** — what symbols mean
- **Compass rose** — which way is north, south, east, west
- **Scale** — how map distance compares to real distance

When you explore a game world, a minimap works the same idea: a tiny guide so you don’t get lost.

articles.subject: history
articles.title: Why Castles Were Built
articles.summary: Stone homes that were also fortresses.
articles.content:
In parts of medieval Europe, powerful families and rulers built **castles**. A castle was more than a fancy house — it was a stronghold.

Castles helped with:
- **Protection** behind thick walls
- **Lookouts** from towers
- **Storage** of food and tools
- **Leadership** — a place to organize people and land

Gates and walls mattered. If a gate stayed locked, only trusted people could enter — a real-life version of needing the right key (or, in a learning game, the right answer!).

articles.subject: history
articles.title: Rivers and Early Towns
articles.summary: How water shaped where people settled.
articles.content:
Many early towns grew beside **rivers**. Water was not optional — it was survival and opportunity.

Rivers offered:
- Fresh water for people and animals
- Fish for food
- Fertile soil for crops in floodplains
- Transport routes for trade

Because rivers connected places, ideas and goods could travel farther. That is one reason maps of old settlements often follow waterways like blue threads.

articles.subject: language
articles.title: Nouns: Naming Words
articles.summary: Words for people, places, and things.
articles.content:
A **noun** is a naming word. It can name:
- A **person** (farmer, friend)
- A **place** (meadow, castle)
- A **thing** (coin, bridge, egg)

In a sentence like “The fox runs,” *fox* is a noun. When you write adventure stories, strong nouns help readers picture your world.

articles.subject: language
articles.title: Beginning, Middle, End
articles.summary: A simple shape for clear stories.
articles.content:
Most satisfying stories have three big parts:

1. **Beginning** — Who is the character? Where are we? What starts the adventure?
2. **Middle** — Problems, choices, and tries (including helpful failures!)
3. **End** — How things change after the challenge

In a learning quest, the “middle” might be a locked gate. A wrong answer is not the end of the story — it is a chance to learn and try again.

articles.subject: technology
articles.title: Algorithms Are Recipes for Problems
articles.summary: Step-by-step thinking used by people and computers.
articles.content:
An **algorithm** is a clear list of steps to finish a task. A cookie recipe is an algorithm. So is a set of directions across a farm.

Computers need algorithms written in languages they understand. Good algorithms are:
- **Clear** (no fuzzy steps)
- **Ordered** (sequence matters)
- **Finishable** (they end)

When a game checks if you answered a quiz correctly, it is following an algorithm too!

articles.subject: technology
articles.title: Simple Machines Help Us Work
articles.summary: Levers, ramps, and wheels make jobs easier.
articles.content:
**Simple machines** help people move things with less effort. Common ones include:
- **Lever** — like a seesaw or crowbar
- **Inclined plane (ramp)** — a slope instead of a tall climb
- **Wheel and axle** — carts and wagons
- **Pulley** — ropes and wheels for lifting

Farm tools, castle gates, and bridges all use these ideas. Technology started with clever helpers, not only with computers.

articles.subject: art
articles.title: Primary Colors
articles.summary: Red, blue, and yellow as building blocks of color.
articles.content:
In paint, **primary colors** are often red, blue, and yellow. You can mix them to make many other colors:
- Red + yellow → orange
- Blue + yellow → green
- Red + blue → purple

Artists also use light and dark, and warm colors (reds/oranges) versus cool colors (blues/greens). Looking carefully at color helps you notice the world — and draw it better.

articles.subject: art
articles.title: Landscape Pictures
articles.summary: Art that shows outdoor places.
articles.content:
A **landscape** is art that shows outdoor scenery — hills, meadows, rivers, skies, and paths.

Artists choose:
- What is close (large, detailed)
- What is far (smaller, softer)
- Where the horizon line sits

Isometric game views are a special way of drawing places with depth. Even when a world is made of tiles, artists still think about light, color, and readable shapes.

articles.subject: math
articles.title: Counting in the Garden
articles.summary: Practice adding and subtracting with plants and animals.
articles.content:
Math lives outdoors too!

- If you plant **4** seeds and plant **3** more, you planted **7** seeds (4+3).
- If a nest has **5** eggs and **2** hatch, **3** eggs are left (5−2).

When you explore, try counting fence posts, flowers, or coins. Counting is the start of bigger math adventures.

articles.subject: math
articles.title: Area of a Rectangle
articles.summary: How to measure space inside a rectangular garden.
articles.content:
The **area** of a shape is how much flat space it covers.

For a **rectangle**:
**Area = length × width**

Example: a garden plot 8 meters long and 3 meters wide has area 8 × 3 = **24 square meters** (m²).

Units matter: meters × meters make square meters. Area helps farmers plan planting space and builders plan floors.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Four Seasons
articles.summary: Spring, summer, autumn, and winter in simple terms.
articles.content:
Many places on Earth have four **seasons**:
- **Spring** — plants wake up; many flowers bloom
- **Summer** — warmer days; lots of growth
- **Autumn (fall)** — leaves may change color and drop
- **Winter** — colder weather; some animals rest or adapt

Seasons change because Earth is tilted as it travels around the Sun. You do not need the full astronomy yet — just notice how the world looks different across the year!

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Deciduous and Evergreen Trees
articles.summary: Two common strategies trees use through the year.
articles.content:
**Deciduous** trees shed leaves in a cold or dry season. Dropping leaves helps them save water and survive tough weather. In autumn many deciduous leaves turn bright colors before falling.

**Evergreen** trees keep leaves (often needles) year-round. Needles can handle cold and dry conditions better in many climates.

Both strategies work. Forests and meadows often mix plant types, which supports more kinds of animals.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Patterns Help Us Predict
articles.summary: Seeing order in numbers, nature, and stories.
articles.content:
A **pattern** is something that repeats in a predictable way. Examples:
- Numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8…
- Nature: day and night
- Music: a beat that returns

Scientists look for patterns to make good guesses about what happens next. In a game, patterns help you learn rules — including when a gate opens after you succeed.

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: North, South, East, West
articles.summary: The four main directions.
articles.content:
The four main directions are:
- **North**
- **South**
- **East**
- **West**

A compass points toward magnetic north to help travelers. On many maps, north is toward the top. Learning directions helps you describe where things are: “the river is south of the cottage,” for example.
